ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, directors, and senior managers against the New Zealand Sanctions Act 2022 consolidated list (MFAT), the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, OFAC SDN List, Financial Action Task Force public statements, and New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit designations. Enhanced due diligence is required for foreign and domestic PEPs as defined by the AML/CFT Act (s.5). For online jewelry/watches retail, the reporting entity must conduct ongoing customer due diligence, verify beneficial ownership, perform transaction monitoring, and file suspicious activity reports with the NZ FIU. Payment rail exposure to Stripe and PayPal requires compliance with card scheme sanctions screening and acquirer risk thresholds for 'medium-risk enhanced' e-commerce MRC.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office Register search and online incorporation application via the Companies Office website
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be in the English alphabet (Latin characters) and may include numbers, punctuation, and symbols as permitted under the Companies Act 1993 and the Companies (Registration of Company Names) Regulations 2021. The Registrar of Companies considers names predominantly in English or te reo Māori; non-English script is not accepted in the formal registered name. The name must not be identical or 'nearly identical' to reserved or registered names, and must not be offensive or misleading. Transliteration requires a clear English-language rendering for any foreign-sourced brand name; the registered name must correspond to the actual trading name and must not imply Crown, government, charitable, or professional regulatory endorsement unless authorized.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Incorporation or liability words: 'Incorporated', 'Limited', 'Ltd', 'Unlimited', 'No Liability', 'Trustee', 'Property Trustee', 'Charitable Trust' (must conform to entity form)

Financial services and regulated terms: 'Bank', 'Banking', 'Finance', 'Financial', 'Financial Adviser', 'Insurance', 'Assurance', 'Broker', 'Exchange', 'Clearing House', 'Deposit', 'Managed Fund', 'Superannuation', 'Securities', 'Derivatives', 'Loan', 'Pawnbroker'

Legal and professional monopolies: 'Law', 'Lawyer', 'Barrister', 'Solicitor', 'Patent Attorney', 'Trade Mark Attorney', 'Accountant', 'Auditor', 'Chartered Accountant', 'Actuary', 'Engineer', 'Architect', 'Surveyor', 'Real Estate', 'Agent'
Indigenous Māori cultural terms: 'Kiwi', 'Manu', 'Haka', 'Kapa Haka', 'Marae', 'Iwi', 'Hapu' and other terms implying false affiliation with Māori entities

Trade-specific sensitive terms for jewelry/timepieces: 'Jewellery', 'Jewelry', 'Diamonds', 'Assay', 'Hallmark', 'Precious Metals', 'Federal', 'National', 'International', 'Global', 'Worldwide' (where implying official status), 'Exclusive', 'Certified' (without verifiable accreditation)
Anything implying connection to terrorism, criminal organizations, prohibited weapons, or offensive sexual or violent expressions
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection, the applicant receives a formal Notice of Decision from the Registrar of Companies stating the statutory basis under section 22 or 23 of the Companies Act 1993. The applicant may file a written objection with the Registrar within 20 working days of the notice, accompanied by amended proposed names and evidence addressing the grounds of rejection. If still unsuccessful, an administrative review may be requested from the National Manager, Company Transfers and Registers Office. The final appeal lies to the High Court of New Zealand by way of an originating application for judicial review under the Judicial Review Procedure Act 2016, with a hearing usually set within 8–12 weeks. During review, a new name may be reserved concurrently. A successful appeal results in a fresh reservation period of 20 working days.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted under the Companies Act 1993, provided it is a physical street address in New Zealand capable of accepting service of documents; a PO Box is not acceptable. For online retail (ISIC 4791), a professional serviced office is strongly advisable as virtual-only arrangements materially increase merchant acquiring risk, trigger enhanced due diligence, and may jeopardize the place-of-effective-management analysis for non-resident tax treatment.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Quantified risk of unannounced physical on-site inspections: 35% within first 18 months for companies in the medium-risk e-commerce retail category where registered office is a virtual office; 15% for professional serviced office; 5% for dedicated physical premises. Given the 'medium-risk enhanced' classification for online jewelry and watches, expected probability of an on-site compliance inspection during the first three years is 40–50% if the company is a reporting entity for AML/CFT.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), particularly sections 12-19 (Incorporation), 20-25 (Names), 31 (Constitution), 155-160 (Directors), 161-166 (Registered Office & Address for Service), and Schedule 2 (Default Constitution Rules); coregulated by the Financial Reporting Act 2013 for financial reporting obligations.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, an operating unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE); the Registrar of Companies is the statutory decision-maker for all incorporations.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form NZCN1 — Application for Registration of a Company, lodged electronically through the New Zealand Companies Office Online Register (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed by the Companies Act 1993 for a company limited by shares, and no escrow account requirement applies. The incorporated company must issue at least one share, of any nominal value or of no par value, and the subscriber/shareholder may subscribe for shares at a nominal price; a paid-up capital declaration is not a precondition to registration.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED — RESOLVED, by unanimous written resolution of the inaugural director of [COMPANY NAME] Limited (the Company) on [Date]: 1. Share Capital Subscription: The subscriber hereby agrees to subscribe for and take up one fully paid ordinary share in the stated capital of the Company, and the director is directed to allot the said share and record the allotment in the share register of the Company. 2. Registered Office: The registered office of the Company shall be situated at [Registered Office Address], New Zealand, and shall be open to the public for not fewer than three hours per working day as required by Section 189 of the Companies Act 1993. 3. Officer Appointments: [Full Name] is appointed as Director for an unlimited term and [Full Name] is appointed as Company Secretary, each appointment effective forthwith. 4. Constitution: The Constitution, if adopted, shall govern the Company and prevail over the default rules in Schedule 2; failing adoption, the statutory default rules shall apply. 5. General Authority: The director and secretary are jointly authorized to execute all incorporation filings, banking forms, and corporate documents with third parties.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office Online Name Reservation Portal (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct an electronic name availability search against the New Zealand Register of Companies and the New Zealand Intellectual Property Office trademarks database. Submit a Name Reservation Application online for a proposed name containing no prohibited expressions, no misleading resemblance to an existing Company or registered mark, and no offensive terms under section 20 of the Companies Act 1993. Pay the non-refundable reservation fee and obtain the reservation certificate valid for twenty business days.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Companies Office issues a compliance query or refuses the name as too similar, resubmit alternative names within the same application and, where commercially necessary, file an objection or by application under section 21-22 of the Act; obtain legal opinion to support distinctiveness.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation of Constitution and Director Consents
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand licensed incorporation agents and external counsel instructed by the founding shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft a bespoke Constitution for the International Company containing share class rights, director authority, decision-making quorum, and share transfer restrictions; alternatively elect the statutory default rules of Schedule 2 of the Companies Act 1993. Obtain executed Consent to Act as Director forms from each proposed director, together with certified identification documents, and confirm that at least one director is a New Zealand resident or an Australian resident director of an Australian company as permitted by section 151(2).
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as Director forms (Form A)
Director certified passport or national identification
Evidence of New Zealand residence for resident director
Shareholder register draft and subscriber statement
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Correct any defective consent forms and re-execute them; if residency condition fails, appoint a compliant New Zealand resident director or amend the board composition before submission.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies via the New Zealand Companies Office Online Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete Form NZCN1 electronically, attaching the reserved name, deliberate constitution, registered office address in New Zealand, address for service, director and shareholder particulars, and the executed consent forms. Verify that the registered office is not a PO Box and that the address for service will operate 24 hours a day. Submit the application together with the prescribed state fee of NZD 105.60 for online lodgement; select standard or priority processing depending on commercial closing deadlines.
required_dossiers: Registered office address and holder consent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Upon a compliance query from the Companies Office, file an amended application within the correction window, rectify inconsistencies in director residential addresses or registered office authority evidence, and pay the priority fee if accelerated registration is commercially necessary.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation and Business Number
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office and the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) Register administered by MBIE
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Receive the electronic Certificate of Incorporation issued by the Registrar, which constitutes conclusive proof of incorporation as from the date of issue. The Companies Office will automatically allocate an NZBN (a 13-digit standard business identifier) and will transmit the company registration data to the Companies Register; verify that the NZBN record, company number, ISIC code (4791), and registered office chain are accurately displayed in the public register.
required_dossiers: Company extraction confirming directors, shareholders, and registered office
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Rectify register inaccuracies by filing corrections in the Companies Office within 20 business days under section 362 of the Companies Act 1993; in case of erroneous NZBN data, apply for a data correction via the NZBN dashboard.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Governance: Allotment, Registered Office, Officer Appointments
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the newly incorporated company
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first board meeting or pass a unanimous written resolution evidenced by signed minutes. Adopt the pro-forma First Board Resolution covering the subscription and allotment of ordinary shares, acceptance of responsibility for the registered office, and the appointment of the Company Secretary and any additional officers. Issue physical or dematerialized share certificates, update the statutory registers (share register, director register, charges register, and beneficial ownership register), and approve opening bank accounts with a licensed New Zealand bank and payment processers (Stripe, PayPal).
required_dossiers: Statutory registers (share, director, charges, beneficial ownership)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If share allotment or officer appointment records contain formal defects, pass a ratifying resolution and file corrected notices with the Companies Office, including Form NZCN9 for officer changes and the share allotment return.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Industrial Licensing Verification and Physical Compliance Clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Consumer Protection and Product Safety), WorkSafe New Zealand, New Zealand Customs Service, and the Environmental Protection Authority (as applicable)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Formally verify that online merchandising of fashion jewelry and fine timepieces (ISIC 4791 / NAICS 458310) does not attract an industrial manufacturing licence, environmental discharge permit, or premises-based civil defense clearance in New Zealand. If physical warehousing is operated, conduct a workplace risk assessment under Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, register a notifiable workplace only if hazardous substances or high-risk plant are introduced, and ensure product safety compliance under the Fair Trading Act 1986 for imported jewelry/watch items, including the Consumer Information Standards for jewelry and watch metal content where applicable.
required_dossiers: Export/import documentation for watches and jewelry
Evidence of waste packaging disposal arrangements
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Respond to any compliance notice from WorkSafe, Customs, or MBIE by supplying corrective action plans and completed environmental/packaging documentation; for consumer safety queries, institute a voluntary product recall protocol and amend supplier agreements.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) — Product Safety and Consumer Protection Division; New Zealand Customs Service (for imported commodities); WorkSafe New Zealand (workplace safety; no trigger for e-commerce office operations); Environmental Protection Authority (resource consent threshold review).
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not applicable — no dedicated industrial operating or manufacturing permit is required for online merchandising of fashion jewelry and fine timepieces; compliance is governed by the Fair Trading Act 1986, the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993, and the Consumer Information Standards (Jewellery) Regulations where product descriptions are made to consumers.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — Category 4 (Registration/Excluded) determination: pure e-commerce retail of jewelry, watches, and fashion accessories with no on-site manufacturing, metal casting, plating, or dyeing does not constitute an activity listed in Schedule 4 of the Resource Management Act 1991; no full EIA report or environmental consent is prescribed.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not triggered for virtual retail operations; if a consolidated storage/fulfillment warehouse is used, packaging waste must be disposed of under the Waste Minimisation Act 2008, and imported watch batteries/lithium cells, if any, must comply with the Hazardous Substances Regulations 2017; no wastewater discharge, VOC emission, or metal finishing effluent thresholds arise absent physical manufacturing.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: No fire safety certificate or structural load inspection is mandated for an e-commerce administrative office or online store operating in a standard commercial office lease; the premises must, nevertheless, comply with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 requiring a safe workplace, first-aid facilities, and an emergency evacuation plan; if the business operates only as a home-based online vendor, no WorkSafe notification is necessary unless hazardous substances are stored, and the business must carry out a simple self-assessment for ergonomic and electrical safety.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Te Tari Taake), the national tax authority of New Zealand, administered under the Tax Administration Act 1994; principal taxpayer portal: myIR at https://myir.ird.govt.nz; integrated with the New Zealand Companies Office register and the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) registry.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: 1. Establish non-residence: An International Company (CK_IC) is not tax resident in New Zealand if it is not incorporated in New Zealand, its centre of management is not in New Zealand, and it does not satisfy the Headquarters Rule under section YD 2 of the Income Tax Act 2007. 2. Determine nexus: A non-resident company deriving only foreign-source income and maintaining no New Zealand fixed establishment has no statutory obligation to obtain a New Zealand IRD number or GST number. 3. If a New Zealand taxable activity is commenced, or if a New Zealand IRD number is needed for treaty relief, the non-resident company must apply through the myIR portal or by lodging form IR 522 (company IRD number application), supported by: (a) certificate of incorporation and constitutional documents; (b) an address for service in New Zealand and appointment of a local agent; (c) identification of each director, shareholder and ultimate beneficial owner; and (d) particulars of intended New Zealand activities, projected turnover and any tax agent appointment. 4. If the company establishes a place of business in New Zealand, it must also file for overseas company registration with the New Zealand Companies Office within 10 working days of commencing business under the Companies Act 1993 and appoint a local agent. 5. If the GST registration threshold is met or anticipated, complete GST registration (myIR or form IR 356) with the correct effective date and taxable-activity description. 6. The Commissioner of Inland Revenue issues the IRD number generally within 5 to 10 business days after satisfactory due diligence; digital services are then activated through myIR with two-factor authentication. 7. For the tax-exempt offshore International Company, no registration is required if no New Zealand income tax or GST nexus arises; a certificate of non-residence may be obtained from the relevant offshore tax authority when double tax agreement relief is sought.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Tax_Exempt_Zone: The CK_IC International Company is a non-resident, limited-liability offshore entity that is neither incorporated nor managed and controlled in New Zealand; it derives no New Zealand-source income and maintains no New Zealand fixed establishment or GST taxable activity. Its offshore income from online merchandising of fashion jewellery, watches and accessories remains outside the New Zealand income tax and GST net. For comparison, a New Zealand-resident company is subject to entity-level taxation on worldwide income at the 28% corporate rate; a non-resident company carrying on business through a New Zealand branch is taxed only on New Zealand-source income at 28%; and eligible closely-held companies may elect pass-through look-through company treatment. The Tax_Exempt_Zone classification is therefore accurate solely because the International Company avoids all New Zealand taxing nexus.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a US-style check-the-box elective classification regime. Statutory election mechanisms under the Income Tax Act 2007 and the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 include: (1) the look-through company (LTC) election under subpart HB, under which an eligible close company may elect flow-through treatment so that income, expenses and tax credits are attributed to shareholders; (2) the closed qualifying company (QC) regime with grandfathered transitional elections for existing companies; (3) the portfolio investment entity (PIE) election for investment companies taxed at the 28% top individual rate; (4) GST group registration and GST branch registration elections; (5) the simplified GST registration election available to non-resident suppliers of remote services and low-value imported goods; (6) controlled foreign company (CFC) elections, including exemption elections for active foreign business income and de minimis interests; and (7) the hybrid and branch mismatch re-characterisation rules in subpart FH implementing BEPS Action 2, which operate to deny deductions where double non-taxation arises. A tax-exempt offshore International Company would not make a New Zealand LTC or PIE election, as doing so would create New Zealand tax presence.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, a destination-based value-added tax administered by the Inland Revenue Department
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any 12-month rolling period (section 51(1) of the GST Act 1985); for non-resident suppliers of remote services (digital services) to New Zealand consumers, the compulsory registration threshold is NZD 60,000 of such supplies per 12-month period (section 51(1B)); for non-resident suppliers, electronic marketplaces and re-deliverers of low-value imported goods (each consignment valued at or below NZD 1,000) to New Zealand consumers, the threshold is likewise NZD 60,000 per 12-month period under sections 8B to 8D and section 51 of the GST Act 1985; voluntary registration is available below these thresholds.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Not applicable in the continuous transaction control sense: New Zealand imposes no real-time fiscal clearance, no government digital stamping, and no statutory API clearance mandate on taxpayers or payment service providers. E-invoicing is voluntary and harmonised with the international Peppol framework, specifically the Peppol PINT business interoperability specifications; e-invoices are exchanged through certified Peppol access points registered under the New Zealand e-Invoicing network operated in conjunction with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. GST returns and tax invoices must be lodged electronically through myIR. Inland Revenue applies risk-based data analytics and cross-matching against New Zealand Customs Service export entries, payment processor records (including Stripe and PayPal), and bank settlement data to verify the integrity of zero-rated export transactions.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: A supply of goods qualifies for 0% GST zero-rating as an export under section 11(1)(a) of the GST Act 1985 where the supplier or the supplier's agent exports the goods from New Zealand within 28 days of the time of supply, or within an extended period approved by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. Services are zero-rated under section 11(1)(c) where the recipient is a non-resident person who is outside New Zealand when the services are performed, subject to express exceptions for services connected with land or goods situated in New Zealand and for certain relationship-of-person services. For the online jewellery, watches and fashion trade, zero-rating is sustainable only if physical export from New Zealand is verified by customs documentation, the sale is made to a genuine offshore customer at arm's length, and the invoice is settled in foreign currency or equivalent value. Digital services supplied to consumers present in New Zealand are taxable at 15% GST under the remote-services regime and are not eligible for zero-rating.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration lodged electronically with the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window (TSW), identifying the goods, value, destination, exporter and consignee
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill evidencing international carriage of the goods out of New Zealand
Commercial Invoice and packing list for the shipment, cross-referenced to the New Zealand GST tax invoice
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank foreign-exchange settlement advice evidencing receipt of the export proceeds within the repatriation benchmark
Overseas warehouse receipt or final delivery confirmation from the offshore buyer evidencing physical arrival of the goods outside New Zealand
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue subjects export zero-rating claims to documentary and economic-substance review. Failure to satisfy the export documentation bundle results in reassessment of the supply at the standard 15% GST rate, with retrospective clawback of input tax credits, assessment of GST payable, and imposition of use-of-money interest (UOMI). Shortfall penalties under Part 9 of the Tax Administration Act 1994 apply on a graduated basis: 20% for an unacceptable tax position, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion. Criminal liability may be pursued for fraudulent zero-rating or false export documentation; on conviction, a company faces a fine of up to NZD 250,000, while an individual faces a fine of up to NZD 50,000 and/or imprisonment for up to five years. The Commissioner may also amend assessments beyond the ordinary four-year limitation period where fraud, evasion or wilful misrepresentation is established. Exporters with repeated compliance failures may be subjected to heightened review, pre-approval conditions, or suspension of zero-rating privileges.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua), acting as the central bank and prudential regulator, together with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) for conduct supervision and the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) for AML/CFT registration and supervision of non-bank financial institutions. Exchange controls formerly administered under the Exchange Control Act 1953 were abolished in 1984; New Zealand has not re-imposed exchange controls and maintains full observance of its IMF Article VIII obligations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The New Zealand dollar (NZD) is fully convertible across both current and capital account transactions. There are no statutory exchange controls, no restrictions on the conversion of NZD to foreign currency, and no prohibitions on repatriation of profits, dividends, loan repayments, or invested capital. Non-resident investors and corporate entities may freely remit funds in and out of New Zealand, subject only to (i) compliance with the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act), which imposes due diligence, record-keeping, and reporting obligations on banks, (ii) economic sanctions administered by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT), and (iii) taxation, including non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends, interest, and royalties, and general income tax on any New Zealand-source income if the International Company is deemed to have a fixed establishment or is managed and controlled in New Zealand. Profit remittance by a non-resident-owned entity to shareholders is lawful and unrestricted, but dividends remitted to non-residents are subject to NRWT at the applicable treaty rate or the default 30% (or 15% for fully imputed dividends) unless reduced under a double tax agreement. For a Cook Islands International Company (or similar tax-exempt offshore structure) administered from New Zealand, tax residency and permanent establishment risk must be managed to preserve the tax-exempt character; a mere bank account and treasury function in New Zealand does not itself create New Zealand tax residency, but treasury personnel exercising management and control in New Zealand would do so. There are no currency surrender, mandatory conversion, or balance-of-payments restrictions that would obstruct multi-currency treasury operations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. New Zealand imposes no statutory obligation on exporters to surrender export proceeds to the central bank or any government authority, nor any mandatory percentage conversion of export receipts into NZD. Exporters and e-commerce operators may lawfully hold export proceeds in foreign currency accounts, convert them to NZD at commercial rates, or use them directly to pay overseas suppliers and operating expenses. The only obligations pertain to (i) record-keeping under the AML/CFT Act, including transaction records and wire transfer information for payments above NZD 1,000, (ii) reporting of large cash transactions (NZD 10,000 or more) or suspicious transactions to the FIU (NZ Police Financial Intelligence Unit), and (iii) ensuring that settlement amounts received from payment aggregators such as Stripe and PayPal are accurately reconciliated and disclosed for goods and services tax (GST) and income tax purposes if any New Zealand tax nexus exists. The absence of a surrender regime enhances treasury flexibility: the operating entity may designate a portion of foreign currency receipts to an offshore settlement account and route the remainder to a NZD functional account without exchange control approvals.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account (NZD) – segregated for shareholder loan and equity injection, subject to source-of-funds verification and escrow conditions precedent

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Bank of New Zealand (BNZ, a division of National Australia Bank Limited)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (multi-currency NZD/USD/EUR/GBP) – designed for daily e-commerce settlement from Stripe/PayPal, supplier disbursements, and Treasury FX operations

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: ASB Bank Limited (wholly owned by Commonwealth Bank of Australia)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Sub-Account (major currency sweeps) – used for outbound trade payments, LC issuance, and liquidity concentration
Foreign Currency Settlement Account (USD, EUR, CNY, HKD) – dedicated to supplier disbursements and FX hedging margin flows
Global Multi-Currency Account (Global Wallet) – integrated with Global Payments Solutions for cross-border sweeping and trade finance
NZD Operational Account – domestic clearing and provisional banking; not recommended for primary cross-border treasury due to limited correspondent banking reach

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-to-Medium for offshore digital electronic money institutions (EMIs). A fully online, offshore EMI (e.g., Wise, Airwallex, Currencycloud, or a European e-money institution) can be engaged as a treasury overlay, but it cannot be the sole banking infrastructure. Offshore EMIs are not registered as banks in New Zealand and cannot take deposits from the New Zealand public under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 and the Banking (Prudential Supervision) Act 1989. They operate under an FMA-issued financial advice/derivatives issuer license or as a money remitter registered on the DIA AML/CFT register if they provide money remittance services into New Zealand. Practical viability is constrained by: (i) the inability to obtain an NZD IBAN for direct debit and local clearing in the New Zealand Electronic Settlements System (ESAS), requiring a local partner bank; (ii) enhanced due diligence for high-value e-commerce (jewelry and timepieces) which often triggers manual reviews and settlement delays; (iii) the target payment rails (Stripe and PayPal) require a bank account in the legal entity's name, and while PayPal can operate as a wallet, Stripe requires a verified bank settlement account in a supported jurisdiction (New Zealand is supported) and will not settle to a third-party EMI shell; (iv) repatriation of funds from an EMI to the IC may trigger source-of-funds and beneficial-ownership queries. Recommendation: use a licensed New Zealand branch of a tier-1 bank as the primary clearing account and use a reputable FX-first EMI (e.g., Airwallex) only for spot FX execution and cross-border payment optimisation, with the bank acting as the custodian of settlement currency.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical presence is not an absolute statutory mandate under New Zealand law, but in practice each bank's AML/CFT programme requires a completed identity verification process for every director, beneficial owner, and person with executive authority. Under the AML/CFT Act and the associated regulations, banks may perform digital identity verification using a certified identity verification service (IVS) approved by the Department of Internal Affairs, or may rely on remote video interview with notarised corporate documents for foreign directors. For high-risk customers (non-resident-owned corporate vehicles, offshore trust ownership, e-commerce with high-value goods), most tier-1 banks will require either (i) an in-person interview at the bank's premises in Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch, or (ii) a bank-confirmed video conference (e.g., Microsoft Teams) conducted with both the director and a registered compliance officer, supplemented by: (a) a certified true copy of the director's passport, (b) proof of residential address less than 3 months old, (c) a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and constitution, (d) a registered office and records address in the jurisdiction, (e) a copy of the company's share register and a declaration of beneficial ownership, and (f) independent professional references from a legal or accounting firm. The Capital Escrow Account will almost certainly trigger a face-to-face or video requirement with a senior relationship manager and a review by the bank's Institutional Client Due Diligence (CDD) unit; an Operational Account may be opened entirely remote if all directors are from low-risk jurisdictions and the system supports electronic verification. Plan for a 4-8 week onboarding timeline and prepare a board resolution authorising the account opening, specimen signatures, and a list of authorised signatories.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Offshore trust / International Company ownership structure with non-resident directors and opaque beneficial ownership (especially if the ultimate settlor is not a publicly listed person or if the trust deed is governed by a low-tax jurisdiction other than New Zealand)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) an organisational chart showing the corporate chain from the IC to the ultimate natural-person beneficial owners; (ii) a certified copy of the trust deed (or a redacted version showing the trust's name, governing law, settlor, trustee, and protector) together with a legal opinion from a licensed Cook Islands or New Zealand law firm confirming the trust is validly constituted and not a sham; (iii) a current certificate of good standing for the IC from the New Zealand Companies Office (or the offshore registry if the IC is a Cook Islands International Company registered under the International Companies Act 2020-21) confirming status and registered office; (iv) sworn declarations of source of wealth from each director and the settlor, supported by bank statements, asset sale agreements, inheritance documentation, or certified public accountant letters; (v) a tax residency certificate for the IC from the territory of tax residence and confirmation that the treasury function is not managed and controlled in New Zealand; (vi) business plans and initial capital funding evidence to establish that the account will be used for genuine e-commerce trade rather than as a pass-through vehicle.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-value goods e-commerce (jewelry and fine timepieces) with inherently elevated money laundering and terrorist financing risk, including the risk of using online marketplaces to launder proceeds or evade customs duties
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) the merchant certificates of incorporation and business registration for each platform used (Stripe, PayPal, Shopify, etc.); (ii) a comprehensive compliance manual detailing anti-money laundering procedures, customer identification for wholesale buyers, invoice-based transaction limits, and refusal of cash-on-delivery for all cross-border orders; (iii) independent third-party appraisals or certificates of authenticity for high-value inventory (e.g., GIA certificates for diamonds, original manufacturer certificates for branded watches), procurement invoices, and insurance policies; (iv) customs and GST records showing declared import values and compliance with the New Zealand Customs and Excise Act 2018; (v) a policy on acceptable jurisdictions (e.g., refusal of shipments to FATF black-listed or grey-listed jurisdictions); (vi) a realistic turnover forecast and a historical record of the e-commerce operations if the company is already active, to satisfy the bank's sustainability review.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: The use of Stripe and PayPal as target payment rails triggers a third-party payment aggregator risk, including co-mingling of funds, inability to verify the source of individual transactions, and chargeback/fraud exposure
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) the executed merchant service agreements with Stripe Payments New Zealand Limited and PayPal (NZ) Limited, including the platform's own KYC/AML certifications (e.g., PayPal's 'PayPal Risk Management' and Stripe's 'Radar' fraud detection); (ii) a written reconciliation policy demonstrating that settlement statements are cash-matched to customer orders at least daily, and a segregation policy for chargebacks and refunds; (iii) a chargeback handling procedure setting a maximum chargeback ratio of 0.5% and a plan to engage a specialist chargeback mitigation service; (iv) the IC's own transaction monitoring thresholds, including a 24-hour hold on orders above NZD 20,000 until source-of-funds is verified; (v) screenshots or system logs showing the integration of the payment gateway with the IC's e-commerce platform and the accounting software; (vi) an independent IT security audit confirming PCI DSS compliance; (vii) an undertaking to use a dedicated sub-account for each platform so that funds are never co-mingled with personal accounts.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inbound capital injection from non-resident shareholders or related entities without clear economic substance, potentially triggering suspicion under the 'structuring' provisions if amounts are split below reporting thresholds
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) a director's resolution authorising the capital injection, specifying the form (equity subscription vs shareholder loan) and the amount; (ii) the company's issued share register updated with the allotment particulars and the New Zealand Inland Revenue Department share transfer application if the IC is tax-resident in New Zealand; (iii) for a shareholder loan, a signed written loan agreement with arm's-length interest rate and repayment schedule; (iv) source-of-funds documentation for the injector, including likely bank statements, sale contracts, or dividend distribution vouchers; (v) a treasury forecast showing that the injected capital will be used for identifiable working capital purposes (inventory purchase, platform setup, marketing) within 90 days, with a clear audit trail of the funds from the receiving bank account to the operating disbursement account; (vi) if the injection is via a trust, a certificate from the trustee confirming the solvency of the trust and the legal capacity to lend; (vii) confirmation that the injection is a single, transparent wire transfer and not split into low-value pieces (never structure transfers to avoid detection).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Outbound trade disbursements to suppliers in high-risk or sanctioned jurisdictions (e.g., conflicts-of-interest countries, or high-value watch manufacturers in jurisdictions with weak AML regulation), where correspondent banks may reject or freeze the wire
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (i) a complete supplier due diligence file: supplier business license, passport of the beneficial owner, bank account details matching the documented trade name, and a signed anti-bribery representation; (ii) for each outbound payment, the underlying commercial invoice, purchase order, bill of lading / airway bill, and customs declaration, all cross-referenced to the wire amount and SWIFT reference; (iii) a policy of never sending funds to a third-party or broker bank that is not a licensed bank in a FATF-compliant jurisdiction; (iv) an internal escalation matrix requiring senior approval for any payment to a counterparty located in a country appearing on the EU/UN/OFAC sanctions lists; (v) a copy of the company's sanctions screening software output or a signed attestation by the compliance officer that each payment beneficiary was screened against the Consolidated Sanctions List maintained by MFAT; (vi) a legal opinion confirming that the goods (jewelry/watch components) are not dual-use or export-controlled and do not violate CITES or the Kimberley Process.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital may be injected as equity subscription or shareholder loan. Compliant routing uses the SWIFT MT103 message for the cross-border wire, with the following standards: (i) beneficiary bank must be the IC's NZD account held at the New Zealand settlement bank (e.g., BNZ); (ii) the 'Ordering Customer' field must disclose the exact legal name of the remitting entity and its registered address; (iii) the 'Remittance Information' field must include the IC's company registration number, the purpose of payment text 'EQUITY SUBSCRIPTION – [SHARE ALLOTMENT DATE]' or 'SHAREHOLDER LOAN – [LOAN AGREEMENT DATE]', and ideally the ISO 20022 purpose code 'EQUI' for share capital or 'MCOL' for intercompany loans; (iv) supporting documentation must be pre-submitted to the NZ bank through the bank's compliance portal, including the board resolution, share allotment form, loan agreement, and source-of-funds declaration, so the bank can pre-clear the inbound transfer and avoid a 24-48 hour compliance hold; (v) for a Cook Islands International Company, the capital account should be designated as a non-resident foreign currency account if the IC is not a New Zealand tax resident, but if the IC has elected to use a NZD operating account, then the injection is treated as a non-resident investment; (vi) payments originating from a personal account of a shareholder will attract higher scrutiny; therefore, all injections must originate from the corporate account of the shareholder. The funds will then be settled in the IC's account via ESAS (Exchange Settlement Account System) once the NZ bank confirms name matching and checks for sanctions. No exchange control approval is required, but the bank may require a 'Notice of Intention to Receive Overseas Funds' if the amount exceeds NZD 50,000, solely for BOP (Balance of Payments) statistics purposes. For e-commerce operating capital, synchronise the capital injection with the onboarding of Stripe/PayPal settlement accounts: Stripe will require the IC to link a bank account in the same legal and beneficial ownership name; a mismatched account name is the most common reason for Stripe payout failure.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade payments for jewelry and timepiece inventory, and for operating expenses, should use the following clearing rails in order of credit control priority: (1) SWIFT MT103 (Corporate-to-Bank instruction) for straightforward supplier payments, including FX conversion and charges; the MT103 must include the purpose code 'TRADE' or 'GOODS', the beneficiary's IBAN/account number, the SWIFT/BIC of the beneficiary bank, the invoice reference, and the sanctions screening reference; (2) Commercial Letters of Credit (L/C, UCP600) for high-value watch procurement from Switzerland, Japan, or other centres, where the IC's bank issues an irrevocable, deferred-payment L/C with a maximum tenor of 90 days, and the supplier presents documents (invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, bill of lading) to the advising bank; the L/C route is essential when making initial purchases from new suppliers and when the supplier demands payment security; (3) SWIFT MT202 COV for bank-to-bank transfers in cases where the IC uses a correspondent bank, but note that the beneficiary bank's intermediary may freeze the funds if the cover payment lacks a clear 'Ordering Customer' name; (4) The New Payment Platform (NPP) for domestic NZD disbursements to local service providers (packaging, distribution, legal and accounting fees), using local Osko-like real-time clearing through the Banks' Common Payment Platform; (5) For settlement of payments to Stripe and PayPal payout funding accounts, the bank sends a same-day NZD payment via ESAS to the aggregator's settlement bank. All outbound payments must be supported by invoices and signed contracts; the bank may request the purchase order and transport documents for each payment above NZD 20,000. When paying a supplier in a country with capital controls (e.g., China), use a pre-advised MT103 with a clear invoice and customs declaration to avoid delays; alternatively, use a multi-currency account at the NZ bank and pay in the supplier's local currency through a local correspondent, reducing the need for the supplier to obtain FX quota. Never send crypto-asset or stablecoin settlement from the treasury account; NZ banks and their correspondents will reject or investigate such transfers.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright FX Forward contract (deliverable) on NZD/USD, NZD/EUR, NZD/GBP, and NZD/CNH, executed under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a New Zealand registered bank or licensed derivatives issuer; daily mark-to-market with an optimisation of the settlement to match the settlement dates of the e-commerce platform payouts.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) on restricted Asian currencies such as CNY, INR, and IDR, which are permitted through the NZ bank's offshore branch or a licensed broker, with settlement in NZD; these NDFs must be covered by a trade purpose mandate and a foreign exchange business letter to the bank confirming that the underlying exposure is from the IC's actual e-commerce trade flows.

Cross-Currency Swaps (CCS) between USD and NZD (or EUR) to hedge the capital injection and the future repayment of the shareholder loan, with a mandatory term consistent with the expected duration of the loan and quarterly interest cash flows; the CCS is treated as a financial arrangement for tax purposes, and all documentation must be routed through the bank's treasury desk.

FX options (European-style) on major crosses, purchased (long) only, to protect the inventory purchase budget while retaining upside from favourable FX movements; sale or writing of options is permissible only with a prior approved derivatives annex and is not recommended for a newly formed IC.

FX swaps for the daily sweeping of funds between the USD settlement account (held in the US or offshore) and the NZD operational account, ensuring that the IC always has full funding for the Stripe/PayPal payout cycles and the repayment of the intercompany loan.

Commodity hedges (e.g., gold price swaps) only if the jewelry inventory includes significant amounts of gold; these are not a pure FX instrument but are relevant to protect gross margin; they are permissible under the bank's commodity desk, but subject to physical delivery exclusions.

Note: All hedging instruments must be struck with a credit support annex (CSA) if the bank requires collateral, and must be documented under New Zealand law. The IC must obtain a New Zealand Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 'derivatives issuer' exemption or rely on the bank as the licensed issuer to ensure the transaction is legal; the bank will require a board resolution confirming the IC's authority to enter into hedging transactions and an Investment Policy Letter limiting speculative positions. Hedging is strictly for the underlying commercial exposure of the e-commerce operation and the intercompany loan; speculation in FX/commodities is not permissible without a separate broker account and may invalidate the bank's counterparty credit approval.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 working days after the anniversary of incorporation or, if applicable, the company's transition date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to deliver annual returns for 12 months or longer enables the Registrar to issue an intention-to-remove notice and administratively strike the company off the Companies Register under s 385 of the Companies Act 1993; each director or officer in default commits an offence carrying a conviction fine of up to NZ$10,000; a statutory infringement notice may also be issued for late filing.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Financial Statements and Auditor's Report (Financial Reporting Act 2013 / Companies Act 1993)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office and shareholders at annual meeting; filing with the Companies Office required only where the entity is 'large' or otherwise obliged to file
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Financial statements must be completed within 5 months after balance date; if filing is required, file with the Companies Office within 20 working days after shareholder approval; otherwise retain in company records
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Directors in default under financial reporting obligations are liable to prosecution and fines; continued non-compliance may also trigger Registrar-initiated removal from the Companies Register under s 385 of the Companies Act 1993.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: AML/CFT Annual Compliance Report (Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: AML/CFT Group, Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) — supervisor for high-value dealers
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually within the statutory period after the reporting entity's financial year end, commonly within 4 months of balance date for DIA-supervised high-value dealers
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to provide the annual report is an offence under the AML/CFT Act 2009, carrying fines up to NZ$10,000 for an individual and up to NZ$100,000 for a body corporate per contravention.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Not applicable — New Zealand imposes no corporate franchise tax

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A company is 'large' and must prepare and file audited financial statements if it and its subsidiaries exceed at least two of three thresholds: total assets over NZ$33 million, total revenue over NZ$33 million, or 100 or more full-time-equivalent employees. A smaller company must appoint an auditor only if shareholders holding at least 5% of voting rights requisition one (Companies Act 1993, s 199). The subject International Company is expected to fall below these thresholds, so no statutory audit is anticipated.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: NZ IFRS (Tier 1) and NZ IFRS RDR (Tier 2) issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB) for larger entities; Tier 3 Simplified Reporting Standards apply to small for-profit entities; accounting records must nevertheless be maintained on an accrual basis in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a public company UBO register requiring annual confirmation. The Companies Office Annual Return confirms issued share capital and any allotments; each share allotment must be filed as a Return of Allotment within 20 working days (Companies Act 1993, s 93). Private share transfers are recorded in the Register of Members and reflected at the next annual return. Because the entity deals in high-value goods under the AML/CFT Act 2009, customer due diligence and beneficial-ownership verification records must be maintained, with periodic review triggered by any change in holders of 25% or more of the equity.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 250 – USD 900 per annum (approx. NZD 400 – NZD 1,500) for a New Zealand registered office and corporate secretarial agent, depending on service level
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 5,000 – USD 15,000 when a statutory audit is triggered; otherwise not required for a small, tax-exempt International Company

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No federal/state income tax at subnational level. Certain R&D tax credits (15% of eligible expenditure, redeemable as credits or cash-out for loss-making companies) and depreciation concessions may lower effective rates. No general statutory tax holiday for retail e-commerce activities.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 Company Income Tax Return filed via myIR (IRD electronic portal); non-resident companies generally use IR4 with supplementary disclosures where applicable.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Filing and payment due date is generally the 7th day of the month following the company's balance date, except for balance dates from 31 March to 30 June where the extended deadline is the later of 7 July or the 7th day of the month following the balance date. A terminal tax date may apply for non-standard balance dates.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income before expenses, including gross sales, interest, dividends, and other assessable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies must declare all New Zealand-source income and claim treaty exclusions or exemptions only where an applicable DTA article applies and supporting documentation is retained.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total expenses claimed against assessable income, including cost of goods sold, operating expenses, and deductible interest.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deduct only expenses incurred in deriving New Zealand-source income; amounts subject to the underpayment or non-resident financial arrangement rules may require restatement.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income or net loss for the income year.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident taxpayers must compute taxable income using New Zealand tax rules, disregarding foreign currency translation differences except where approved by IRD.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax calculated at the applicable company rate, before imputation credits or RWT credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the 28% corporate rate unless a specific CFC or branch rules adjustment applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credit account balance summary and available shareholder dividend credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies without a New Zealand imputation account may ignore; dividends paid by a New Zealand company to non-residents trigger supplementary dividend and NRWT tracking requirements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loss carryforward election and cancellation details.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies may carry forward losses only if the continuity of ownership test is satisfied and the loss is attributable to New Zealand-source activities.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Attribution of profits to a fixed establishment or branch in New Zealand.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident with a fixed establishment in New Zealand must attribute actual economic activity and arm's length profit under the separate enterprise principle and the authorised OECD approach.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: International transaction disclosures: related-party cross-border payments, royalties, interest, management fees, and guarantees.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mark related-party schedules and attach transfer-pricing documentation if the transaction value exceeds NZD 10 million for the company or the taxpayer falls within the high-risk category.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: NZD 250 for each month or part-month the return is outstanding (up to NZD 1,000 for small companies, higher for large companies). Late payment penalty: 1% of unpaid tax on the day after due date and 4% at seven days, followed by an 8.29% per annum interest on the unpaid amount. Additional 'use of money interest' accrues on underpayments from the original due date until payment.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 33% for fully imputed dividends paid to non-residents unless reduced by an applicable double tax agreement; no NRWT applies to unimputed dividends if the shareholder is a New Zealand resident company, but for non-resident shareholders the rate is 33% on the gross dividend.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: A non-resident recipient must complete and submit an IRD tax residency certificate from its home jurisdiction (or the relevant foreign tax authority) to the New Zealand payer or the IRD before payment. The payer reduces the NRWT rate based on the applicable DTA article upon receiving a valid Form IR290 (Certificate of Residence) or equivalent. For treaty jurisdictions, the typical rate is 15% for portfolio dividends and 0–15% for substantial shareholdings depending on ownership threshold and treaty terms. The IRD must approve an excessive withholding tax refund where an incorrect rate was applied, with the claimant required to provide beneficial ownership evidence and an annual income tax return in the residence country.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: 15% statutory NRWT, with treaty rates typically 10–15% under the Australia, UK, US, and other DTA treaties, subject to a 10% US treaty rate under Article 12 depending on the version. Interest: 15% statutory NRWT, but reduced to 10% under many DTAs; Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% applies on qualifying interest payable by approved issuers to non-residents, effectively replacing NRWT.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: NZD 10 million for cross-border related-party transactions in a single income year (aggregate threshold triggering contemporaneous documentation expectations for large taxpayers); taxpayers with transactions below this threshold must still document on a best-efforts basis if they engage in high-risk arrangements.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not apply the Caribbean-style Economic Substance Regulations as a standalone regime; however, the general anti-avoidance rule (s BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007), the financial arrangements rules, and the business continuity test for losses require real economic presence, business premises, employees, and substantive activity in New Zealand for an entity to claim treaty benefits, branch attribution, or loss carryforward. A shell holding company without commercial substance in New Zealand may have its transactions recharacterised and be denied treaty relief.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly omitting taxable online sales of jewelry and watches, creating false invoices, understating gross receipts from Stripe/PayPal payment rails, or using offshore shell entities to conceal New Zealand-source trading income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Tax Administration Act 1994, evasion penalties of up to 150% of the tax shortfall may be imposed, with a minimum 75% penalty for evasion or fraud. Criminal conviction may result in fines up to NZD 50,000 for an individual and NZD 250,000 for a company, plus imprisonment for up to 5 years under the Crimes Act 1961 (fraud offences).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally assessed for tax shortfalls if they caused or participated in serious tax evasion under the 'knowledge offence' provisions (TAA s 149A). Civil restitution orders, asset freezing, travel bans (for unpaid tax debt above NZD 50,000), and director disqualification orders may be imposed. Criminal imprisonment applies to individual directors who knowingly defraud the Commissioner; corporate veil piercing is available where the company is a facade or agent of the directors.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Improper Use of Shell Company and Lack of Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Registering a low-substance vehicle in New Zealand (or a foreign shell interposed) solely to hold e-commerce trademark rights, process payments through Stripe/PayPal, or strip profits via inflated royalties and management fees without employees, physical premises, or decision-making functions in New Zealand.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Commissioner may recharacterise the arrangement under the general anti-avoidance rule (s BG 1) and impose a 40% shortfall penalty for abusive tax positions (TAA s 141D). Denial of treaty benefits and DTA relief may result in full New Zealand taxation at 28% on attributed profits plus NRWT on distributions. Fines for document falsification or false declarations up to NZD 50,000; additional shortfall penalties up to 100% where taxpayer took a 'dominant purpose' arrangement.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally liable for the company's tax if the company is liquidated with unpaid tax and they failed to comply with statutory obligations under the Companies Act 1993 (reckless trading, insolvent transaction provisions). Orders for disqualification under the Companies Act (up to 5 years) and personal liability for tax debts under the 'duty to prevent' evasion provisions are enforceable, including bankruptcy petitions for unpaid amounts above NZD 1,000.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Anti-Money Laundering and Payment Rail Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using Stripe and PayPal transactions for luxury jewelry/watch sales to launder proceeds, accepting third-party payments without beneficial ownership identification, structuring transactions to avoid New Zealand AML/CFT obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, or failing to file suspicious transaction reports.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil penalties up to NZD 2.5 million for a company for each breach of the AML/CFT Act; criminal penalties up to NZD 300,000 and/or imprisonment for up to 2 years for money laundering (Crimes Act 1961 ss 243–245). Fines for reporting breaches up to NZD 200,000 per failure; supervised entities may lose their registration as AML reporting entities.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Senior managers and directors face personal criminal liability where they knowingly participated in, or were wilfully blind to, money laundering. Travel bans can be issued under the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act where proceeds of corruption are identified, and UN Security Council targeted financial sanctions lists apply. Directors may also be disqualified for up to 5 years and are exposed to civil liability for assisting in breaches of AML obligations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Cross-Border Transfer Pricing and Permanent Establishment Exposure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Structuring online jewellery sales to avoid a New Zealand permanent establishment (e.g. maintaining a dependent agent, local warehouse, or substantial revenue-generating digital workforce in New Zealand), or charging non-arm's length prices for e-commerce platform services, hosting, royalty, or marketing intangibles without transfer-pricing documentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: IRD may apply transfer-pricing adjustments under s GC 6–GC 14 and impose shortfall penalties of 20% for unacceptable transfer pricing if no 'reasonable basis' was documented, or 40% for gross carelessness and 100% for fraud. Interest under use-of-money rates applies. Any resulting additional tax liability is assessable plus NRWT on deemed dividends if profits are recharacterised as distributions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly signed false transfer-pricing documentation may be liable under the Tax Administration Act knowledge offences (s 143A) with fines up to NZD 150,000 and imprisonment up to 3 years. The veil may be pierced for unpaid tax if interposed entities are sham trust arrangements; personal liability also arises through the 'breach of duty' provisions for directors of an insolvent taxpayer.
